title: Trump commutes James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served
description_short: On January 19, 2021, Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served, directed release, and left supervision and unpaid fine balance in effect.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s 480-month federal prison sentence to time served and directed the Bureau of Prisons to release him immediately upon receipt of the warrant. The warrant left any unpaid portion of his $25,000 fine, a $100 assessment, and his five-year supervised-release term with all conditions intact. It described April 10, 2034 as his projected release date before the commutation; it does not document when release was carried out.
description_long: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump signed a commutation warrant for James Brian Cruz, whose 2001 Western District of Texas sentence included 480 months in prison, five years of supervised release, a $25,000 fine, and a $100 special assessment. The warrant commuted the prison sentence to time served. It directed the Bureau of Prisons to effect Cruz’s immediate release upon receipt of the warrant, with all possible speed. The document said his projected release date had been April 10, 2034, describing the date he might otherwise have remained confined, not recording when he was actually released. It expressly left in effect any unpaid fine balance, the $100 assessment, the five-year supervised-release term with all its conditions, and all other components of the sentence. This was a commutation of imprisonment, not a pardon erasing the conviction. The warrant establishes the terms ordered but does not provide a separate release record or evidence of later compliance with supervision conditions.

proposal.description_long: The Justice Department records that President Donald Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s sentence on January 19, 2021. Cruz had been convicted in the Western District of Texas in 2001 of conspiring to possess more than 500 grams of methamphetamine with intent to distribute. The clemency list gives the original sentence as 480 months in prison, five years of supervised release and a $25,000 fine. The recipient-specific commutation warrant states that the prison sentence was reduced to time served and notes a then-projected release date of April 10, 2034. This fills the key gap in the prior account: the warrant specifies the practical change to the prison term. The action was a commutation, not a pardon; the source does not say the conviction was erased. The list identifies supervised release and the fine as elements of the original sentence, while the warrant’s operative language addresses the prison sentence. It does not provide a separate release record or detail post-release supervision terms. The revised title and descriptions therefore state the reduction supported by the warrant and avoid claims about a release date or supervision outcome beyond what the available official documents say.
